title: Hardening and Configuration
objective: By the end of this lesson you can build a hardened baseline, explain secure boot and disk integrity, and shrink an endpoint's attack surface with configuration, including disabling what nobody uses.

blocks.text: A baseline is a documented, tested configuration standard: services off, ports closed, logging on, password policy set. Machines are compared against the baseline, and drift is corrected. A golden image bakes the baseline into the machine template itself, so every new system starts hardened, identical, and reproducible.

items: Endpoint hardening: EDR agents, host firewall on, local admin rights removed, full-disk encryption enabled.
Disabling unused services, ports, and protocols: everything switched on is a door; switch off what no one uses.
Patch management: scan, prioritize, test, deploy, verify; unsupported systems get isolated instead.
Group policy and MDM: enforce the baseline centrally rather than by hand.

blocks.text: Secure boot lets firmware verify the operating system loader's signature before running it, blocking bootkits. A TPM chip stores keys and measurements of the boot chain, so secrets stay sealed unless the machine boots into a known-good state. Self-encrypting drives and full-disk encryption protect data at rest; measured boot and remote attestation let a server prove its boot state to another machine.

rows: Close what serves no purpose; retire Telnet, FTP, SMBv1
Restrict or block USB storage by policy
Remove or rename default accounts; no permanent local admin
Turn on logging before an incident, with time sync

blocks.title: On the exam
blocks.text: Hardening questions reward the smallest sufficient change: the scenario names a system with unnecessary services running, and the answer disables the unused service, rather than adding another product. End-of-life systems get isolation or replacement, because no patch will come.

blocks.title: Write a five-line baseline
steps: Choose a system you know: a laptop, a server, or a router.
Write five baseline items as checkable statements, for example 'SSH service enabled, Telnet disabled'.
Mark each item as enforced by group policy, MDM, or manual check.
Keep it; the asset-management lesson will add classification and disposal to this list.
blocks.expected: Five statements a second person could verify true or false by looking at the machine, each with an enforcement mechanism named.

cheatsheet: Baseline = documented, testable configuration standard; golden image = baseline baked into the deployment template.
Turn off unused services, ports, and protocols; every enabled feature is reachable surface.
Secure boot verifies the loader; TPM seals keys to a known-good boot state; attestation proves it remotely.
Full-disk or self-encrypting drives protect data at rest; removal policy protects data in motion.
Unsupported systems: isolate or retire, because patches will never arrive.

checkpoint.prompt: A file server still offers Telnet, FTP, and SMBv1 alongside its current services. The quickest hardening win is to:

choices.B: Move the server behind two more firewalls
choices.C: Disable the unused legacy protocols and services

checkpoint.explanation: Switching off what nobody uses removes the exposure outright. Extra products and longer passwords defend doors that could instead be closed.
